purpose: Transfers electrical control signals across a barrier of complete physical isolation using light. Inside a light-tight chip, an infrared LED shines onto a phototransistor. Because there is zero copper connection between input and output, lethal 240V mains surges or high-power motor noise can never physically reach your microcontroller.

whenToUse.scenario: Commercial Relay Modules (The JD-VCC Safety Jumper)
whenToUse.why: When mechanical relays click, their electro-magnetic coils kick back nasty voltage transients. An optocoupler on the module isolates the Arduino's delicate GPIO pin from the noisy coil power supply.
whenToUse.recommended: PC817 (4-pin DIP, found on virtually every Arduino relay board)

whenToUse.scenario: Interfacing with 24V Industrial PLCs & Factory Sensors
whenToUse.why: Industrial machinery standardizes on 24V DC logic. Feeding 24V directly into a 5V Arduino or 3.3V ESP32 pin instantly incinerates the silicon. An optocoupler safely reads 24V pulses while outputting clean 5V/3.3V to the MCU.
whenToUse.recommended: PC817 or EL817 with a 2.2 kΩ current-limiting resistor

whenToUse.scenario: AC Mains Zero-Cross Detection & Light Dimming
whenToUse.why: To dim an AC incandescent bulb or control an electric heater with a TRIAC, the Arduino must detect the exact moment the 240V AC sine wave crosses 0V. An optocoupler safely signals this microsecond pulse with 5,000V isolation.
whenToUse.recommended: 4N35 / H11AA1 (AC input optocoupler) or MOC3021 (random phase) / MOC3041 (zero-cross)

whenToUse.scenario: Breaking Ground Loops & Audio Hum in Studio/MIDI Gear
whenToUse.why: When separate audio or musical devices share common ground wires, stray currents create an audible 50Hz/60Hz ground hum. The MIDI specification mandates optoisolation on all inputs to guarantee silence.

basics.title: How it works inside
basics.text: Pins 1 & 2 are connected to an internal infrared LED. Pins 3 & 4 (or 4 & 5) are connected to a silicon phototransistor. When your Arduino pin goes HIGH, the internal LED glows. Photons strike the phototransistor base, causing it to conduct. Light carries the signal — electricity never touches!

basics.title: Current Transfer Ratio (CTR)
basics.text: The optical gain ratio between output collector current and input LED forward current: CTR = (I_C / I_F) * 100%. A typical PC817 has a CTR of 50% to 300%.

basics.title: Active-Low Pull-Up Output
basics.text: The phototransistor output is normally wired between your Arduino input pin and GND, with an internal or external 10kΩ pull-up resistor. When the input LED lights up, the phototransistor pulls the Arduino pin LOW.

types.name: Phototransistor Output (PC817, 4N35)
types.summary: Standard DC optocoupler. Simple 4-pin or 6-pin DIP package. Switches up to 50mA DC at moderate speeds (up to 80 kHz).
types.applications: Arduino relay modules, DC motor isolation, 24V PLC input boards

types.name: Photo-TRIAC Output (MOC3021, MOC3041)
types.summary: Drives AC loads directly or triggers external power TRIACs (BTA16, BTA41) for controlling 110V/240V AC lamps, fans, and heaters.
types.applications: Mains light dimmers, AC solid-state relays (SSR), heater controllers

types.name: High-Speed Logic Output (6N137, HCPL-2601)
types.summary: Features a built-in logic gate and amplifier capable of handling 10 Mbps data rates. Used for isolated serial communications.
types.applications: Isolated RS-485 Modbus, CAN bus isolation, MIDI musical instrument interface

types.name: Darlington Output (4N32, 6N138)
types.summary: Dual transistor output providing ultra-high sensitivity (CTR up to 500%). Conducts full output current with just 1mA LED input current.
types.applications: Battery-powered triggers, low-current sensor inputs, MIDI receivers
